22 General Precautions
Not everyone responds well or the same to medication. The age, the habit of use, physical condition of the user or other circumstances may vary the effects of the drugs.

Always consult the doctor or pharmacist.
Use medications properly.
Never self-medicate.
Never mix drugs with alcohol.

(Página 49 del manual 'Learning to drive')

questions.help:
DISTRACTIONS    
   
8 The mobile phone
Carrying a mobile phone in the car can be very useful in case of breakdown or emergency, but their misuse causes a significant increase in road traffic collisions due to distraction.
The danger of having a collision when using a mobile phone, is four times higher than if not used, so it becomes comparable to the risk of driving with alcohol at a rate of 1 g/l in blood.
In Spain the use of a manually held telephone whilst driving is forbidden, due to the hazardous nature of its use. However, the use of hands-free devices is permissible but it does not eliminate the danger of an accident, because the mere act of using the phone leads to the driver’s attention being reduced.
(Página 35 del manual 'Learning to drive')

7 Obligations after a collision
Any one implicated, present or has knowledge of a traffic collision is obligated to:
Help or summons assistance, to attend the victims, (if there are any).

Help re-establish, when possible, the flow and safety of other traffic.
Assist and relay the facts of the situation and how the traffic incident occurred.
Communicate, and inform (in all cases) your identity and that of anyone involved in the collision, when and if requested.

questions.help:
ALCOHOL AND OTHER DRUGS    
   
16.2 Effects of Alcohol
Changes that alcohol produces in the driver’s physical capabilities:
It alters the ability to undertake movements with precision and coordination.
It makes the driver’ coordination more difficult, so that he cannot accurately assess his surroundings and the movement of other road users.
Impact of alcohol on the driver’ decision-making abilities:
It increases the reaction time during which the vehicle will travel further before the driver responds.
It increases the likelihood that the driver will make wrong decisions.
It leads to the driver implementing decisions ineffectively.
(Página 43 del manual 'Learning to drive')

12 Distances  
 
12.3 The stopping distance
The overall stopping distance is the distance the vehicle takes to come to a complete stop from the point at which the driver first sees the hazard to the point the vehicle comes to a final stop. In other words it is the result of adding the reaction distance and the braking distance together.
(Página 179 del manual 'Learning to drive')

12 Distances  
   
12.3 The stopping distance
The stopping distances will always increase if the reaction distance/time or the braking distance increases.
As a result the stopping distance of a vehicle ultimately depends upon its speed. However other factors can additionally have an influence on this.
It can thus be seen that the stopping distance of the vehicle will depend on its speed and the condition of the driver, the road surface and the vehicle itself.
(Página 180 del manual 'Learning to drive')

FACTORS THAT AFFECT PHYSICAL CAPABILITIES  
   
11.3 Effects of drowsiness
Drowsiness / sleepiness:
Increases the reaction time.
Increases the number of distractions behind the wheel, as it prevents the driver from concentrating on traffic.
Alters the ability to make decisions when driving. The driver takes longer to take any decision and makes more errors at the wheel, especially in complicated situations when there is a need to respond quickly.
Alters the mobility of the driver. The muscles relax and movements are slower and less accurate. It is also common to notice a tendency to execute movements automatically, without thinking sufficiently.
(Página 39 del manual 'Learning to drive')

questions.help:
12 Distances
 
12.1 The reaction distance
The reaction distance is the distance travelled by the vehicle from the time of seeing a hazard until he reacts to it.
It is dependant on the speed and the driver’s reaction time, which in turn depends, on many other factors, such as, the driver’s reflexes, their psycho-physical state (level of alertness, whether or not the driver is under the influence of alcohol etc.) Even the environment can affect the time it takes for a driver to react to any given circumstance (the passenger compartment temperature, noise, etc.)
A reaction time of 0.75 seconds is considered to be normal, during which time the vehicle will travel a distance, determined by the speed at which the vehicle is travelling.
(Página 179 del manual 'Learning to drive')

12 Reflective markers
 
12.1 Obligatory fitment of reflectors
Motorcycles and mopeds with two wheels will generally have one obligatory reflector fitted to the rear. However, vehicles with three or more wheels (three-wheeled moped, light quadricycles, motorcycles with a trailer) are required to have one or two reflectors fitted to the rear.
Trailers and semi-trailers must have two reflectors fitted to the front and two, red triangular, reflectors on the rear, with the option of having two extra red (non triangular) reflectors on the rear if its width exceeds 2.10m (the optional reflectors are not applicable to agricultural trailers).
It is also obligatory, if the vehicle exceeds 6 metres in length, to have 2 lateral reflectors fitted to the sides.
(Página 104 del manual 'Learning to drive')

questions.help:
Road traffic collisions  
   
1 A public health problem
Moreover, in addition to the human drama, it is important to highlight the enormous economic impact (either directly or indirectly) that occurs as a result of a traffic collision.
Costs derived from road traffic accidents are classified as human, material, healthcare and administrative.
Human costs include the loss of lives, productive capacity and physical and psychological suffering. Material costs consist of damages caused on vehicles and their loads as well as on the road and the environment. Healthcare costs comprise first aid, care and treatment of the wounded, rehabilitation and adaptations. Administrative costs hold those of police officers and firefighters and insurance and services management.
People believe that an accident has little effect on them but the cost is borne by taxpayers. The cost of vehicle insurance is also affected, as premiums are affected by collision data and the cost of accidents.
For these reasons, various international organisations, including the World Health Organisation (WHO), believe that road collisions are a priority public health problem throughout the world.
There is a serious need to work together to reduce the high numbers of dead and seriously injured on the roads.
(Página 248 del manual 'Learning to drive')

questions.help:
1 Speed    
 
1.2 Is it dangerous to speed?
Although speed is one of the main factors of a collision, the severity and consequence is relative to the speed travelled when the collision occurs. For example the likelihood of a fatality occurring in a traffic collision is 60 % higher when driving at a faster speed than when driving at an adequate speed.
It has been estimated in various studies that a reduction of one kilometre per hour in average speed would reduce the number of fatal collisions by 3 %.
(Página 171 del manual 'Learning to drive')

Avoid a possible accident; such as in narrow roads, hump back bridges or roads with bends with little or no visibility.
